figures.name: Tertullian
figures.dates: born c. 155-160; writing 196/197 to after 220; Jerome says he lived to a decrepit old age
figures.places: Carthage, Roman Africa (modern Tunisia); knew Rome and wrote some works (lost) in Greek
figures.role: Convert from paganism in adult life; the first great Latin Christian writer; apologist, controversialist and moralist; coined much of the West's Trinitarian vocabulary. Jerome calls him a presbyter, but in his own writings he speaks as a layman ("Are not even we laics priests?"), so his ordination is doubted.
figures.status_note: Not venerated as a saint in any church. From about 207 he embraced the New Prophecy (Montanism) and by about 211-213 had withdrawn from the catholic majority, whom he called "Psychics" (unspiritual); his own words: "We indeed, on our part, subsequently withdrew from the carnally-minded on our acknowledgment and maintenance of the Paraclete" (Against Praxeas 1). Jerome says he "lapsed to the doctrine of Montanus" (Illustrious Men 53); Vincent of Lerins calls him "a great trial in the Church" (Commonitory 18). Augustine reports a small "Tertullianist" group in Carthage that returned to the church in his day (De haeresibus 86; reported in the Catholic Encyclopedia, not read in the Latin here). Works after c. 207 (On Modesty, On Fasting, On Monogamy, On Flight) attack the church he had defended, so always mark early versus Montanist-period views. His Trinitarian formulas (trinitas, una substantia, tres personae) were later accepted as orthodox. Reader cautions: his harshest lines on women ("the devil's gateway") and his gloating picture of the damned (The Shows 30) are genuine and will offend.
figures.hook: He wrote a whole book urging Christians to be patient, and opened it by confessing that he himself was "ever sick with the heats of impatience".

stories.story: Cyprian, bishop of Carthage a generation later, never let a day pass without reading Tertullian, and would say to his secretary, "Give me the master", meaning Tertullian. Jerome heard this from an old man who had been Cyprian's secretary.
stories.source: Jerome, Illustrious Men, chapter 53 (NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, tr. E. C. Richardson)

stories.story: At an imperial handout in the camp, every soldier wore the laurel crown except one, who carried it in his hand. Asked why, he said, "I am a Christian", took off his cloak and boots, gave up his sword and went to prison. Other Christians called him rash for endangering a long peace over "a mere matter of dress"; Tertullian wrote The Chaplet to defend him and sneered that the critics' pastors were "lions in peace, deer in the fight".

Tertullian tells of a Christian woman who went to the theatre and came home possessed. When the demon was rebuked in the exorcism for attacking a believer, it answered, "And in truth I did it most righteously, for I found her in my domain."

In his congregation was a woman who fell into ecstasy during Sunday worship, conversed with angels and sometimes the Lord, and afterwards reported her visions to the leaders, who examined them carefully. One vision showed her a soul in bodily shape, "soft and transparent", which Tertullian used as evidence in his book On the Soul.
stories.source: A Treatise on the Soul (De Anima), chapter 9

stories.story: Warning the governor Scapula, he recalled that when Arrius Antoninus persecuted in Asia, all the Christians of the province presented themselves at his tribunal together; the governor executed a few and told the rest, "O miserable men, if you wish to die, you have precipices or halters." Tertullian asks what Carthage would do if its thousands did the same.
Mocking the crowd that blamed every flood, drought and plague on Christians ("Away with the Christians to the lion!"), he asked: "What! shall you give such multitudes to a single beast?"

Before any sign of death, he wrote his wife a letter-treatise telling her not to remarry after he died, assuring her it was not jealousy since there will be no marriage in the resurrection, and ending with one of the warmest pictures of Christian marriage in early literature.
stories.source: To His Wife, Book 1 chapter 1 and Book 2 chapter 8

stories.story: He began life as a pagan who laughed at Christian belief himself: "Once these things were with us, too, the theme of ridicule. We are of your stock and nature: men are made, not born, Christians."

When Carthaginians mocked him for giving up the Roman toga for the Greek philosopher's cloak (pallium), he wrote a whole witty pamphlet in which the cloak itself speaks up for a quiet life away from the forum.

temperament.evidence: "So I, most miserable, ever sick with the heats of impatience, must of necessity sigh after, and invoke, and persistently plead for, that health of patience which I possess not"

temperament.trait: Vehement and forceful; everyone who knew his work said so
temperament.evidence: Jerome: "a man of keen and vigorous character" (Illustrious Men 53). Vincent of Lerins: "Every word almost was a sentence; every sentence a victory" (Commonitory 18).
temperament.source: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53; Vincent of Lerins, Commonitory 18

temperament.trait: Savage wit and ridicule of opponents, which he defended on principle
temperament.evidence: "Vain and silly topics are met with special fitness by laughter. Even the truth may indulge in ridicule, because it is jubilant; it may play with its enemies, because it is fearless." Of Marcion: "What Pontic mouse ever had such gnawing powers as he who has gnawed the Gospels to pieces?"

temperament.trait: Proud to stand with the minority, and unembarrassed at changing his mind
temperament.evidence: "As if it were not easier to err with the majority, when it is in the company of the few that truth is loved!" and "I blush not at an error which I have ceased to hold, because I am delighted at having ceased to hold it"

temperament.trait: Contempt for timid clergy and compromise
temperament.evidence: "I know, too, their pastors are lions in peace, deer in the fight."

He refuses any loophole: to a debtor who signed a pagan oath but claims he never spoke it, he answers "Silence of voice is an unavailing plea in a case of writing". The Catholic Encyclopedia notes his close knowledge of Roman legal procedure (identification with the jurist Tertullian is doubtful).
His picture of a Christian couple: "Together they pray, together prostrate themselves, together perform their fasts; mutually teaching, mutually exhorting, mutually sustaining."

genuine_lines.quote: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church? What between heretics and Christians?
genuine_lines.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: See, they say, how they love one another, for themselves are animated by mutual hatred; how they are ready even to die for one another, for they themselves will sooner put to death.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: We are of your stock and nature: men are made, not born, Christians.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: O noble testimony of the soul by nature Christian!
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: We are but of yesterday, and we have filled every place among you
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: The prison does the same service for the Christian which the desert did for the prophet.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: The leg does not feel the chain when the mind is in the heavens.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: He who fears to suffer, cannot belong to Him who suffered.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: Faith fears not famine.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: Prayer is alone that which vanquishes God.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: Nay, the birds too, rising out of the nest, upraise themselves heavenward, and, instead of hands, expand the cross of their wings, and say somewhat to seem like prayer.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: If I should offer you a rose, you will not disdain its Maker.
genuine_lines.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: But we, little fishes, after the example of our ΙΧΘΥΣ Jesus Christ, are born in water, nor have we safety in any other way than by permanently abiding in water
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: That which He Himself has not produced is not pleasing to God, unless He was unable to order sheep to be born with purple and sky-blue fleeces!
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: I blush not at an error which I have ceased to hold, because I am delighted at having ceased to hold it, because I recognise myself to be better and more modest. No one blushes at his own improvement.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: Would you have something of blood too? You have Christ's.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: Is it better to be damned in secret than absolved in public?
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

genuine_lines.quote: Yes, and the Cæsars too would have believed on Christ, if either the Cæsars had not been necessary for the world, or if Christians could have been Cæsars.
genuine_lines.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)

misattributed.line: Credo quia absurdum ("I believe because it is absurd")
misattributed.truth: This Latin formula is not in any of his writings; it became attached to him (and sometimes to Augustine) centuries later. The nearest real line is On the Flesh of Christ 5: "And the Son of God died; it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd. And He was buried, and rose again; the fact is certain, because it is impossible." He was arguing against Marcion, who denied that Christ had real flesh, that the shame of the cross is exactly what no one would invent; it is not a rejection of reason.

misattributed.line: "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church."
misattributed.truth: A later smoothing. The real line is Apology 50: "the blood of Christians is seed" (Latin: semen est sanguis Christianorum).

misattributed.line: "See how these Christians love one another!" quoted as sincere pagan praise
misattributed.truth: Genuine (Apology 39), but Tertullian reports it as what pagans say with a sneer, and turns it: "for themselves are animated by mutual hatred".

misattributed.line: "Woman, you are the devil's gateway" quoted as his general doctrine of women
misattributed.truth: Genuine (On the Apparel of Women 1.1), in a sermon-like appeal to Christian women to dress plainly, addressing them as daughters of Eve. The same author wrote the tender portrait of Christian marriage in To His Wife 2.8. Quote it, but in context.

misattributed.line: Tertullian was a Roman lawyer (the jurist Tertullianus of the Digest)
misattributed.truth: Possible but unproven. Eusebius calls him "a man well versed in the laws of the Romans" (Church History 2.2), and the Catholic Encyclopedia judges it "doubtful" that he is the jurist cited in the Pandects.

misattributed.line: Tertullian was a priest of Carthage
misattributed.truth: Only Jerome says so (Illustrious Men 53). Tertullian writes as a layman: "Are not even we laics priests?" (On Exhortation to Chastity 7). Many scholars now think he was never ordained.

opinions.side_note: Against pagan learning as a source for faith. Irony worth noting: he used Stoic ideas freely (a bodily soul, in On the Soul), and Vincent of Lerins says he "comprehended all philosophy".
opinions.position: Philosophy is the seedbed of heresy; once you have Christ you need no Greek speculation.
opinions.quote: Away with all attempts to produce a mottled Christianity of Stoic, Platonic, and dialectic composition! We want no curious disputation after possessing Christ Jesus, no inquisition after enjoying the gospel! With our faith, we desire no further belief.
opinions.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits people well. Many believers and most secular people think faith should engage philosophy and science; a sizeable minority (some fundamentalists, some mystics) share his suspicion of "clever" theology.

opinions.side_note: A middle position: learn from the world's culture, do not become its salesman.
opinions.position: A Christian child may learn pagan literature at school, but a Christian may not teach it, because teaching means praising the gods in it.
opinions.quote: Learning literature is allowable for believers, rather than teaching; for the principle of learning and of teaching is different.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Very few today would bar Christians from teaching secular subjects; the live version is whether Christians should work in industries whose content they disapprove of.

opinions.side_note: Closed questioning: seek until you find, then stop.
opinions.position: Inside the rule of faith you may ask anything; outside it, endless seeking is itself the mark of heresy. Knowing the creed is knowing enough.
opinions.quote: To know nothing in opposition to the rule (of faith), is to know all things.
opinions.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Divides sharply. Modern culture prizes open-ended questioning; traditional believers of many churches still hold that some questions are settled.

opinions.side_note: Limited second chance. He later withdrew even this for adultery and apostasy (next entry).
opinions.position: EARLY VIEW (c. 203): after baptism God grants one more repentance to a Christian who falls into grave sin, but only once.
opinions.quote: In the vestibule He has stationed the second repentance for opening to such as knock: but now once for all, because now for the second time; but never more because the last time it had been in vain.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Almost no one today limits forgiveness to one relapse; the question splits better as "should there be limits on how often a community takes someone back?"

opinions.side_note: Against second chances for grave sins. He mocks the bishop (probably Callistus of Rome or Agrippinus of Carthage) as "Pontifex Maximus".
opinions.position: MONTANIST VIEW (c. 210-220): the church must not readmit adulterers and apostates; a bishop who announces their pardon is betraying the church.
opinions.quote: The Church has the power to forgive sins; but I will not do it, lest they commit others withal.
opinions.location: chapter 21 (he presents this as the Paraclete speaking through the new prophets)
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Very one-sided today: most Christians and non-Christians believe serious wrongdoers can be restored. Useful as a sharp pole for the rigorist minority.

opinions.side_note: Pure-church side (Montanist period).
opinions.position: The church is a pure virgin bride and must be kept free even from hearing a promise of pardon for adultery.
opinions.quote: Far, far from Christ's betrothed be such a proclamation! She, the true, the modest, the saintly, shall be free from stain even of her ears.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most churchgoers today prefer the "field hospital" picture; a committed minority wants strict membership and discipline.

opinions.topic: new: truth usually lies with the few
opinions.position: Being in the minority is no sign of error; truth is more often loved by the few.
opinions.quote: As if it were not easier to err with the majority, when it is in the company of the few that truth is loved!
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits people interestingly across belief lines: contrarians and converts agree; people who trust consensus and institutions disagree.

opinions.side_note: He wrote this when critics threw his earlier views back at him.
opinions.position: Abandoning an old opinion is improvement, not fickleness, and nothing to be ashamed of.
opinions.quote: I blush not at an error which I have ceased to hold, because I am delighted at having ceased to hold it, because I recognise myself to be better and more modest. No one blushes at his own improvement.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most people say they agree; fewer act on it. Could be sharpened into "Changing your convictions is a sign of strength" versus "of instability".

opinions.topic: new: a church needs no clergy
opinions.position: Every believer is a priest; where there is no ordained clergy, laypeople may baptize and offer for themselves, and three believers make a church.
opinions.quote: But where three are, a church is, albeit they be laics.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits Christians by tradition: many evangelicals and house-church Christians agree; Catholics, Orthodox and many Anglicans hold that a church needs ordained ministry.

opinions.side_note: Detachment from wealth.
opinions.position: Money is not really ours; losing it should not upset us, and people who can lose calmly are the ones who give freely.
opinions.quote: Who fears not to lose, finds it not irksome to give.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most people agree in principle; it splits when framed as "being upset at being robbed is a kind of greed".

opinions.side_note: Voluntary, not compulsory: "there is no compulsion; all is voluntary."
opinions.position: Christians share their goods freely with one another through a voluntary common fund for the poor, orphans, the old, shipwrecked and prisoners.
opinions.quote: One in mind and soul, we do not hesitate to share our earthly goods with one another. All things are common among us but our wives.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Admired by most; few practise it. Splits on "voluntary giving versus a duty to share".

opinions.side_note: For solitude. The second line is spoken by the personified philosopher's cloak in his own satire, but it is his case.
opinions.position: Withdrawal from the crowd is good for the soul: prison can be a hermitage, and the quiet life beats public life.
opinions.quote: The prison does the same service for the Christian which the desert did for the prophet.
opinions.location: chapter 2 (compare On the Pallium 5: "The better life you would more enjoy in seclusion than in publicity.")
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Introverts and contemplatives agree; activists and extroverts disagree. A good splitter.

opinions.side_note: Against mental reservation and technicalities; he forbids oaths entirely ("Christ prescribes that there is to be no swearing").
opinions.position: No technical loopholes: a Christian who signs a written oath cannot excuse himself by saying he never spoke it aloud.
opinions.quote: Silence of voice is an unavailing plea in a case of writing; and muteness of sound in a case of letters.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most people agree that signed words bind; the refusal of all oaths is held today only by Quakers, Mennonites and similar groups.

opinions.side_note: Pleasure redirected rather than denied, but "distaste of pleasure itself" counts as a pleasure.
opinions.position: Christians have their own better pleasures (peace with God, a clear conscience, freedom from fear of death) and need not envy the world's.
opinions.quote: What greater pleasure than distaste of pleasure itself, contempt of all that the world can give, true liberty, a pure conscience, a contented life, and freedom from all fear of death?
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Few today would call "distaste of pleasure" a pleasure; the gentler claim (spiritual joys beat entertainment) splits believers and non-believers.

opinions.side_note: Total abstention.
opinions.position: Christians must stay away from the games, races and theatre entirely; they are idolatrous and inflame the passions.
opinions.quote: Would you have also fightings and wrestlings? Well, of these there is no lacking, and they are not of slight account. Behold unchastity overcome by chastity, perfidy slain by faithfulness, cruelty stricken by compassion, impudence thrown into the shade by modesty
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Modern analogues (violent films, blood sports, some games) still split Christians; most people today see entertainment as neutral.

opinions.side_note: For calm over stirred feelings. Ironic given his own famously hot temper.
opinions.position: Strong excitement (the kind shows produce) is spiritually harmful; the Spirit is gentle and is grieved by rage and agitation.
opinions.quote: For the show always leads to spiritual agitation, since where there is pleasure, there is keenness of feeling giving pleasure its zest; and where there is keenness of feeling, there is rivalry giving in turn its zest to that.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits people: many value intense feeling (sport, music, drama) as healthy; contemplatives and some therapists value calm.

opinions.side_note: Pacifist side, with a noted shift from his early apologetic.
opinions.position: MATURE VIEW (c. 211): military service is unlawful for Christians; a soldier who converts should leave the army or accept martyrdom. EARLIER (Apology 42, 197) he had boasted "We sail with you, and fight with you", and in Apology 37 that Christians count it "better to be slain than to slay".
opinions.quote: Shall it be held lawful to make an occupation of the sword, when the Lord proclaims that he who uses the sword shall perish by the sword? And shall the son of peace take part in the battle when it does not become him even to sue at law?
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits well: most Christians accept just war or military service; historic peace churches and many others hold to non-violence.

opinions.side_note: Against state-enforced religion (written as a persecuted minority).
opinions.position: Religion must never be compelled; free choice of worship is a natural human right. He is often cited as the first writer to use the phrase "religious liberty" (Apology 24: "by taking away religious liberty, and forbidding free choice of deity").
opinions.quote: However, it is a fundamental human right, a privilege of nature, that every man should worship according to his own convictions: one man's religion neither harms nor helps another man. It is assuredly no part of religion to compel religion
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Nearly universal agreement in the West today, so weak as a splitter unless framed as "should laws reflect Christian morality?"

opinions.side_note: Against Christians in high office.
opinions.position: A Christian can hardly hold high public office: its ceremonies, oaths, judging and punishing are bound up with idolatry, and worldly power is hostile to God.
opinions.quote: Let even this fact help to remind you that all the powers and dignities of this world are not only alien to, but enemies of, God
opinions.location: chapter 18 (compare Apology 21: "the Cæsars too would have believed on Christ, if either the Cæsars had not been necessary for the world, or if Christians could have been Cæsars")
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most Christians today think believers should serve in politics; Anabaptists and some others still keep their distance.

opinions.side_note: Restrained grief.
opinions.position: Since the dead will rise, Christians should long for them but not lament them; unrestrained grief betrays weak faith.
opinions.quote: That which you think to be death is departure. He who goes before us is not to be lamented, though by all means to be longed for. That longing also must be tempered with patience.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Strong split: modern grief culture says mourning should be expressed freely; many believers still feel "don't grieve like those without hope".

opinions.side_note: Against revenge; he also says "the precept is absolute, that evil is not to be repaid with evil".
opinions.position: Revenge is never justified; leave it to God. Patience even robs the attacker of his enjoyment.
opinions.quote: Whereas, if I shall repose on patience, I shall not feel pain; if I shall not feel pain, I shall not desire to avenge myself.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most agree revenge is wrong; many dispute that patience makes you stop feeling the pain.

opinions.side_note: High view of Christian marriage (though elsewhere he ranks celibacy higher, To His Wife 1.3).
opinions.position: Marriage between two believers is a shared life of prayer, service and song that delights Christ; a believer should marry only a believer, even if that means marrying down in wealth.
opinions.quote: Together they pray, together prostrate themselves, together perform their fasts; mutually teaching, mutually exhorting, mutually sustaining.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most Christians agree marriage should be a spiritual partnership; "marry only a believer" and "marry a poor believer over a rich unbeliever" split people.

opinions.topic: new: remarrying after a spouse dies
opinions.position: A widow or widower should not remarry; he formally asked his own wife not to after his death. (Later, as a Montanist, he called second marriage a kind of adultery in On Monogamy.)
opinions.quote: The precept, therefore, which I give you is, that, with all the constancy you may, you do, after our departure, renounce nuptials; not that you will on that score confer any benefit on me, except in that you will profit yourself.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Very one-sided today: almost everyone thinks remarriage after bereavement is fine. Some Orthodox practice (no remarried priests) keeps a trace of it.

opinions.position: The desire for children is no reason to marry; children are a burden in the last days, and the servant of God has better things to do.
opinions.quote: Further reasons for marriage which men allege for themselves arise from anxiety for posterity, and the bitter, bitter pleasure of children. To us this is idle.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits interestingly: many Christians today treat children as a central blessing and purpose of marriage; many secular people and some celibacy-minded Christians agree children are optional.

opinions.side_note: Calling over family security.
opinions.position: If your trade or livelihood compromises faith, leave it, even when family depends on you; God will provide.
opinions.quote: None of them whom the Lord chose to Him said, I have no means to live. Faith fears not famine.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits people: many would say providing for your family comes first; radical-discipleship Christians agree with him.

opinions.side_note: Against flight, with a documented change of mind.
opinions.position: MONTANIST VIEW (De Fuga, c. 208-212): fleeing persecution is forbidden; clergy who flee are bad shepherds. EARLIER (To His Wife 1.3) he allowed flight as permitted though less blessed.
opinions.quote: I had rather be one to be pitied than to be blushed for. More glorious is the soldier pierced with a javelin in battle, than he who has a safe skin as a fugitive.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Very one-sided: nearly everyone thinks escaping danger is legitimate; the live version is whether leaders may leave their people in a crisis.

opinions.topic: new: paying your way out of trouble
opinions.position: Buying off persecutors with bribes is just flight with money, and an insult to Christ who ransomed you with His blood.
opinions.quote: but that you should ransom with money a man whom Christ has ransomed with His blood, how unworthy is it of God and His ways of acting
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most people today would pay a bribe to escape unjust persecution; a principled minority would refuse.

opinions.side_note: Strongly ascetic in later life; mocks the catholics as gluttons ("love shows its fervour in sauce-pans").
opinions.position: MONTANIST VIEW: fasting is a necessary remedy for the sin of Adam, which came by eating; he would treat food as poison and hunger as its antidote. EARLIER (Apology 42) he wrote that Christians "reject no creature of His hands" and only practise restraint.
opinions.quote: Unbidden, I would, in such ways and at such times as I might have been able, have habitually accounted food as poison, and taken the antidote, hunger
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Few today treat food as poison; fasting as spiritual practice splits Christians (Orthodox and Catholics for, many Protestants indifferent).

opinions.side_note: Against universal salvation, emphatically.
opinions.position: The persecutors, pagan kings and scoffing philosophers will burn forever, and the saints will enjoy watching it.
opinions.quote: How vast a spectacle then bursts upon the eye! What there excites my admiration? What my derision? Which sight gives me joy? Which rouses me to exultation?
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: The gloating is one-sided (almost everyone recoils); the underlying belief in eternal punishment splits Christians roughly in half in many surveys.

opinions.side_note: For present-day revelations (a Montanist conviction).
opinions.position: God still gives prophecy and visions in the church today; a woman in his congregation received them in Sunday worship, and they were tested and trusted.
opinions.quote: For, seeing that we acknowledge spiritual charismata, or gifts, we too have merited the attainment of the prophetic gift, although coming after John (the Baptist).
opinions.work: A Treatise on the Soul (De Anima)
opinions.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits Christians: Pentecostals and charismatics (hundreds of millions) agree; cessationist Protestants and many others are sceptical.

opinions.side_note: Creation is good and reveals God (against Marcion). Elsewhere he argues God made all things "out of nothing" against Hermogenes, who held matter eternal (Against Hermogenes 16).
opinions.position: The smallest things in nature (a hedge flower, a shellfish, a bee, a spider's web) prove a good and skilful Creator; despising the material world insults God.
opinions.quote: imitate, if you can, the cells of the bee, the hills of the ant, the webs of the spider, and the threads of the silkworm
opinions.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Broad agreement among believers; splits with those who see nature as indifferent or cruel.

opinions.side_note: Restrained, plain-sense reading of parables.
opinions.position: Do not build doctrine out of details of the parables; interpret the parables by what is already taught plainly, and do not twist every detail into an allegory.
opinions.quote: We, however, who do not make the parables the sources whence we devise our subject-matters, but the subject-matters the sources whence we interpret the parables, do not labour hard, either, to twist all things (into shape) in the exposition, while we take care to avoid all contradictions.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most preachers agree in principle; splits with readers who love finding hidden meanings in every detail.

opinions.side_note: Tradition-first rather than Bible-only argument.
opinions.topic: new: arguing Bible verses with those who reject the church's faith
opinions.position: Do not debate heretics from Scripture at all; Scripture belongs to the church that received the apostolic rule of faith, so settle first who owns it.
opinions.quote: Our appeal, therefore, must not be made to the Scriptures; nor must controversy be admitted on points in which victory will either be impossible, or uncertain, or not certain enough.
opinions.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits Christians by tradition: Catholics and Orthodox lean his way; most Protestants insist on arguing from Scripture.

opinions.position: Some ideas deserve laughter rather than serious refutation; truth may ridicule because it is fearless, provided the mirth is decent.
opinions.quote: Vain and silly topics are met with special fitness by laughter. Even the truth may indulge in ridicule, because it is jubilant; it may play with its enemies, because it is fearless.
opinions.translation: Alexander Roberts, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits well: satirists and debaters agree; people who value gentleness and charity disagree.

opinions.position: Confess serious sin openly before the church; hiding it to save face is foolish, since God sees anyway.
opinions.quote: Is it better to be damned in secret than absolved in public?
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits people: most prefer private confession or none; some communities (and recovery groups) value open confession.

opinions.topic: new: prayer changes what God does
opinions.position: Prayer is powerful enough to prevail on God Himself; it heals, frees prisoners, brings rain and even calls souls back from death.
opinions.quote: Prayer is alone that which vanquishes God.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits believers: many think prayer changes outcomes; others think it changes the one who prays.

opinions.side_note: For quiet prayer.
opinions.position: Pray quietly and modestly; God hears the heart, not the volume, and loud praying only annoys your neighbours.
opinions.quote: The sounds of our voice, likewise, should be subdued; else, if we are to be heard for our noise, how large windpipes should we need! But God is the hearer not of the voice, but of the heart, just as He is its inspector.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits Christians by style: liturgical and contemplative traditions agree; Pentecostal and revivalist traditions pray aloud.

opinions.position: Loving and praying for those who persecute you is the mark that sets Christians apart from ordinary decency.
opinions.quote: For all love those who love them; it is peculiar to Christians alone to love those that hate them.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Widely admired, rarely disputed in principle; splits when made concrete ("pray for those who hurt you before you pray for yourself").

opinions.topic: new: praying for rulers who oppose you
opinions.position: Christians pray constantly for the emperor's long life, a strong army and a peaceful world, even while he persecutes them.
opinions.quote: Without ceasing, for all our emperors we offer prayer. We pray for life prolonged; for security to the empire; for protection to the imperial house; for brave armies, a faithful senate, a virtuous people, the world at rest
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits along political lines today: many find it hard to pray for leaders they oppose.

opinions.topic: new: everyone knows God deep down
opinions.position: The human soul, when it speaks naturally ("God sees", "God will repay"), bears witness to the one God; the soul is by nature Christian.
opinions.quote: O noble testimony of the soul by nature Christian!
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Believers mostly agree; secular people mostly disagree. A clean splitter.

opinions.topic: new: the body matters to God
opinions.position: The flesh is not a prison to escape; it is the hinge of salvation, washed, anointed and fed in the sacraments, and it will rise.
opinions.quote: They cannot then be separated in their recompense, when they are united in their service.
opinions.work: On the Resurrection of the Flesh
opinions.location: chapter 8 (same chapter: "the flesh is the very condition on which salvation hinges")
opinions.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Many Christians today unknowingly hold a body-leaving view of heaven; physical resurrection splits believers from "spiritual" believers.

opinions.side_note: The real source of the "credo quia absurdum" legend.
opinions.position: The shameful and "impossible" parts of the gospel (God crucified, dead and risen) are marks of its truth, because no one would invent them.
opinions.quote: And the Son of God died; it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd. And He was buried, and rose again; the fact is certain, because it is impossible.
opinions.translation: Peter Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits: some believers love the paradox; rationalists and evidentialist Christians dislike it.

opinions.position: Delay baptism, especially of little children; let them come when they can understand and ask for it.
opinions.quote: Let them come, then, while they are growing up; let them come while they are learning, while they are learning whither to come; let them become Christians when they have become able to know Christ.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits Christians roughly in half (Baptists and Pentecostals agree; Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans, Presbyterians baptize infants).

opinions.position: Women may not teach or baptize in church; the Acts of Paul and Thecla, cited to support it, is a forgery whose author was deposed.
opinions.quote: For how credible would it seem, that he who has not permitted a woman even to learn with over-boldness, should give a female the power of teaching and of baptizing!
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits Christians sharply by church; most secular people disagree with him. Note his own church valued a woman prophet (On the Soul 9).

opinions.position: Dyed cloth, cosmetics and jewellery improve on God's work and so come from the devil; Christian women should dress plainly.
opinions.quote: That which He Himself has not produced is not pleasing to God, unless He was unable to order sheep to be born with purple and sky-blue fleeces!
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 4, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: One-sided against him today except in plain-dress communities (Amish, some Pentecostal holiness groups).

opinions.side_note: A useful contrast with his own later rigorism.
opinions.topic: new: Christians living fully in ordinary society
opinions.position: EARLY VIEW (197): Christians are no hermits; they work, trade, sail, farm and serve alongside everyone, rejecting nothing God made. (His later works pull back sharply from army, office and festivals.)
opinions.quote: We are not Indian Brahmins or Gymnosophists, who dwell in woods and exile themselves from ordinary human life.
opinions.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most Christians today agree; monastic and separatist minorities do not.

sparring.over: Whether the Creator of the Old Testament is a lesser god than the Father of Jesus, and whether Christ had real flesh; five books of ridicule and argument
sparring.source: Against Marcion (5 books); On the Flesh of Christ

sparring.over: The Trinity (Praxeas made Father and Son one person) and the New Prophecy (Praxeas persuaded the bishop of Rome to withdraw recognition of Montanus). "he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father."

sparring.with: Hermogenes, a Christian painter of Carthage
sparring.over: Whether matter is eternal or God made all things out of nothing; Tertullian also attacked his art and his repeated marriages, calling him one "who mistakes loquacity for eloquence, and supposes impudence to be firmness"

sparring.with: A bishop he calls "Pontifex Maximus" and "bishop of bishops" (probably Callistus of Rome, possibly Agrippinus of Carthage)
sparring.over: An edict readmitting penitent adulterers and fornicators to communion

sparring.with: The catholic majority, whom he called "Psychics"
sparring.over: Fasting, second marriage, forgiveness, flight in persecution and the authority of the New Prophecy
sparring.source: On Fasting; On Monogamy; On Modesty; On Flight in Persecution

sparring.with: Quintilla, a woman teacher of the Cainite sect in Carthage
sparring.over: Whether baptism with water is necessary ("a viper of the Cainite heresy")
Their cosmic myth of aeons, which he chose to refute largely by ridicule
Whether one may flee persecution; Fabius asked and disagreed

sparring.with: Jerome and Vincent of Lerins (posthumous verdicts)
sparring.over: His move to Montanism: Jerome says envy and insults from the Roman clergy drove him to it; Vincent calls him "more eloquent by far than faithful"
sparring.source: Jerome, Illustrious Men 53; Vincent of Lerins, Commonitory 18

figures.name: Perpetua
also_known_as: Perpetua and Felicity (with her slave companion Felicitas)
figures.dates: born c. 181; martyred 7 March 203, aged about 22
figures.places: Carthage, Roman Africa (modern Tunisia); imprisoned and killed in the military camp amphitheatre at games for the birthday of Geta Caesar
figures.role: Well-born, educated young married woman and nursing mother, a catechumen baptized in prison; kept a prison diary, the earliest surviving writing by a Christian woman.
figures.status_note: Saint and martyr in the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches; named in the Roman Canon of the Mass with Felicity; Catholic feast 7 March. Caution: chapters 3-10 (modern numbering) are her own first-person diary; chapters 11-13 are her fellow martyr Saturus's vision; the frame (preface and death) is by an eyewitness editor. The editor's preface champions new prophecy and visions, so many scholars link the circle to the New Prophecy (Montanism); others see ordinary African Christianity. The editor is sometimes said to be Tertullian; that is unproven. Augustine later warned that the Passion is not Scripture. Her own opinions on everyday life are few: she left a prison diary, not treatises, so her entries are fewer and some rest on the editor's eyewitness report.
figures.hook: A 22-year-old nursing mother kept a prison diary, told her weeping father she could no more stop being a Christian than a water jug could be called something else, and in the arena guided her trembling executioner's hand to her own throat.

stories.story: Her pagan father begged her to recant. She pointed to a water jug and asked if it could be called by any other name. "No," he said. "Neither can I call myself anything else than what I am, a Christian." He lunged at her as if to tear out her eyes, then left.
stories.source: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity, ANF chapter 1.2 (modern chapter 3), her own words

stories.story: Thrown into a dark, crowded dungeon, she was terrified and frantic about her baby. When the deacons bribed the guards and she was allowed to keep her son with her, she wrote that "the dungeon became to me as it were a palace, so that I preferred being there to being elsewhere."

Her brother told her she was now so close to God she could ask for a vision. She promised: "Tomorrow I will tell you." She saw a narrow golden ladder lined with swords and hooks, a dragon crouching beneath it; she trod on the dragon's head as her first step and climbed to a garden where a white-haired shepherd gave her cheese, and woke "still tasting a sweetness which I cannot describe."

In prayer the name of her brother Dinocrates, who had died at seven of a disfiguring cancer, came to her. She saw him thirsty and unable to reach a pool; she prayed for him day and night, and then saw him healed, drinking from a golden bowl that never emptied, and running off "to play joyously, after the manner of children."

The night before the games she dreamed she was led into the arena to fight a hideous Egyptian: "I was stripped, and became a man." She beat him, trod on his head and received a branch of golden apples. She woke understanding that her real fight was with the devil, "Still I knew that the victory was awaiting me."

When the military tribune treated the prisoners harshly, she told him to his face that it was hardly to his credit to bring them out half-starved for Caesar's birthday: "Or is it not your glory if we are brought forward fatter on that occasion?" He blushed and ordered better treatment.

Tossed by a wild cow in the arena, she pulled her torn tunic over her thigh and asked for a pin to put up her hair, "for it was not becoming for a martyr to suffer with dishevelled hair, lest she should appear to be mourning in her glory"; then she lifted up the injured Felicity. Stabbed clumsily by a young gladiator, she cried out and "herself placed the wavering right hand of the youthful gladiator to her throat."

In her fellow martyr Saturus's vision of heaven, their bishop Optatus and the presbyter Aspasius, quarrelling, threw themselves at the martyrs' feet begging them to make peace between them; Perpetua spoke with them under a rose tree, and the angels told the clergymen to forgive one another.

Her slave companion Felicity gave birth in prison two days before the games. Mocked by a guard for crying out in labour, she answered: "Now it is I that suffer what I suffer; but then there will be another in me, who will suffer for me, because I also am about to suffer for Him."

temperament.evidence: "And I, who knew that I was privileged to converse with the Lord, whose kindnesses I had found to be so great, boldly promised him, and said, 'Tomorrow I will tell you.'"
"After a few days we are taken into the dungeon, and I was very much afraid, because I had never felt such darkness."

temperament.trait: Tender toward her family while refusing them
temperament.evidence: "And I grieved over the grey hairs of my father, that he alone of all my family would not rejoice over my passion."
To the tribune: "Or is it not your glory if we are brought forward fatter on that occasion?"

temperament.trait: Composed, dignified and joyful at the end
temperament.evidence: The editor: she "followed with placid look, and with step and gait as a matron of Christ, beloved of God"; she "sang psalms" on the way in.

misattributed.truth: Only the prison diary (modern chapters 3-10) is hers. Saturus wrote his own vision (11-13); an eyewitness editor wrote the preface and the account of the games (1-2, 14-21). Lines like "love one another, all of you" and the hairpin detail come from the editor.

misattributed.line: The Passion was written by Tertullian
misattributed.truth: A frequent claim (because of the style and the pro-prophecy preface), never proven. Tertullian does cite Perpetua's vision of paradise by name (On the Soul 55).

Disputed. The editor's preface defends "modern visions", a New Prophecy theme, but Perpetua herself shows no break with the church: her deacons Tertius and Pomponius serve her, and Saturus's vision honours bishop Optatus while rebuking a church quarrel.

misattributed.line: Perpetua's vision proves unbaptized children can be prayed out of hell
misattributed.truth: Augustine took this up against Vincentius Victor: of Dinocrates "there is no record in the canonical Scripture", and the account never says Dinocrates was unbaptized (On the Soul and its Origin 1.10 [12]).

opinions.side_note: Calling over family.
opinions.position: When faith and family collide, faith wins, even against a loving father's tears and a baby's need, though she grieves for them.
opinions.quote: And Hilarianus the procurator, who had just received the power of life and death in the place of the proconsul Minucius Timinianus, who was deceased, said, 'Spare the grey hairs of your father, spare the infancy of your boy, offer sacrifice for the well-being of the emperors.' And I replied, 'I will not do so.'
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (her diary)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits people strongly. Many believers admire it; many others, including many Christians, think a mother's duty to her infant and her father should come first.

opinions.side_note: Closely related to the lying key: no outward pretence, even for a good cause.
opinions.topic: new: going through the motions to keep the peace
opinions.position: She refuses even a token outward act (a pinch of incense for the emperors' welfare) that would have saved her life and spared her family.
opinions.quote: Neither can I call myself anything else than what I am, a Christian.
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (her diary)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits people: many would perform a meaningless gesture to save a life; others think giving way on small symbolic acts is where integrity is lost.

opinions.side_note: For seeking visions and signs.
opinions.position: You can ask God to show you what is coming, and expect an answer; she did, and read her dream as a clear sign.
opinions.quote: And I, who knew that I was privileged to converse with the Lord, whose kindnesses I had found to be so great, boldly promised him, and said, 'Tomorrow I will tell you.'
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (her diary)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits Christians: charismatic and Pentecostal believers agree; many others are wary of asking God for signs.

opinions.position: Prayer can help those who have already died; she prayed day and night for her dead little brother and saw him freed from suffering.
opinions.quote: But I trusted that my prayer would bring help to his suffering; and I prayed for him every day until we passed over into the prison of the camp
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (her diary)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits Christians roughly in half: Catholics and Orthodox pray for the dead; most Protestants do not.

opinions.topic: new: my life is in God's hands, not mine
opinions.position: Whatever happens on the scaffold is God's will; we are not in our own power.
opinions.quote: On that scaffold whatever God wills shall happen. For know that we are not placed in our own power, but in that of God.
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (her diary)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Believers mostly agree in principle; people who stress personal agency and planning disagree.

opinions.side_note: Feelings admitted, not suppressed (contrast Tertullian on grief).
opinions.position: She records her fear, anguish and grief plainly, without shame, alongside her resolve; courage does not require feeling nothing.
opinions.quote: After a few days we are taken into the dungeon, and I was very much afraid, because I had never felt such darkness.
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (her diary)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Most people today agree that admitting fear is healthy; some still see showing fear as weakness.

opinions.side_note: The other side of the same key: her choice was not coldness.
opinions.position: Motherhood mattered intensely to her: with her baby beside her even a dungeon felt like home, and she arranged his care before she died.
opinions.quote: the dungeon became to me as it were a palace, so that I preferred being there to being elsewhere.
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (her diary)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Universally sympathetic; not a splitter by itself, but it keeps her portrait honest.

opinions.side_note: Reported by the eyewitness editor, not her diary.
opinions.position: Even as a condemned prisoner she demanded decent treatment from the officer in charge, and shamed him into it.
opinions.quote: Why do you not at least permit us to be refreshed, being as we are objectionable to the most noble Cæsar, and having to fight on his birth-day? Or is it not your glory if we are brought forward fatter on that occasion?
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (editor's eyewitness account)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Splits temperaments: many admire speaking up; others think a Christian should suffer quietly.

opinions.side_note: Reported by the editor as her words.
opinions.topic: new: no one may force your conscience
opinions.position: Having come freely, the martyrs refused to be dressed as priests and priestesses of pagan gods; they had given their lives precisely so as not to be forced into such things.
opinions.quote: We have come thus far of our own accord, for this reason, that our liberty might not be restrained.
opinions.work: Passion of Perpetua and Felicity (editor's eyewitness account)
opinions.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1885)
opinions.today: Very broadly agreed in principle today; splits when the cost is high.
