figures.name: Hippolytus of Rome
figures.places: Rome (wrote in Greek); deported in 235 to Sardinia, where he died
figures.role: The most learned theologian of the Roman church in his day: presbyter, biblical commentator, chronologist (his Easter tables are carved on a statue once thought to be his), and relentless heresy-hunter. He refused to accept bishops Callistus and his successors and led a rival community at Rome.
figures.status_note: Saint and martyr in the Catholic Church (feast 13 August, shared with Pope Pontian), the Orthodox Church (as Hieromartyr Hippolytus, Pope of Rome) and the Anglican Communion. Cautions: (1) he was in schism against the recognised bishops of Rome, reconciled only in exile; the list of Roman bishops of 354 records "the exiled bishop Pontianus and the presbyter Hippolytus" deported together in 235, and both were buried at Rome on the same day and honoured as martyrs. (2) The Hippolytus question: scholars debate whether all works under his name are by one man; the Refutation of All Heresies and Against Noetus are the firmest; the Apostolic Tradition is contested (marked below); On the End of the World and On the Twelve Apostles are spurious. (3) His portrait of Callistus is a hostile rival's account. (4) Later legend (Damasus, Prudentius) made him a Novatianist torn apart by horses, which is anachronistic and borrowed from the Greek myth of Hippolytus.
figures.hook: Rome's most learned churchman denounced his own bishop as an embezzling ex-convict, then shared exile in Sardinia with that bishop's successor, and the Church now keeps their feast on the same day.

stories.story: Hippolytus tells how Callistus, later bishop of Rome, began as a Christian slave running a bank for his master; he lost the deposits of widows and fellow believers, fled, and when caught at the harbour threw himself into the sea; he was fished out, sent to the treadmill, caused a riot in a synagogue hoping to die a martyr, and was sentenced to the mines of Sardinia. Hippolytus tells it to discredit him.
stories.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 9 chapter 7 (ANF; 9.12 in modern editions)

stories.story: He says he and his party "reproved and withstood" bishop Zephyrinus to his face, and that Callistus retorted by calling them "Ditheists", worshippers of two gods. Hippolytus in turn called Callistus "an impostor and knave".
stories.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 9 chapters 6-7

stories.story: Exiled in 235 to Sardinia with Pontian, bishop of the church he had opposed, he apparently made peace there; both died on the island, and their bodies were brought back to Rome and buried on the same day, 13 August.
stories.source: Chronography of 354, list of bishops of Rome (entry for Pontianus); Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. Hippolytus of Rome" (1910)

stories.story: Jerome reports that one of his homilies was preached in the presence of the young Origen, visiting Rome, and that Origen's patron Ambrose later urged Origen to write commentaries "in emulation of Hyppolytus" (Jerome's spelling).

He tells of two church leaders who misread prophecy: one in Syria led believers with wives and children into the desert to meet Christ, where they wandered like bandits and were nearly executed by the governor; another in Pontus, trusting his own dreams, announced the Judgment within a year, so his people left their fields and sold their property, and when nothing happened the young women married, the men went back to farming, and those who had sold everything ended up begging.
stories.source: Commentary on Daniel 4.18-19 (Greek text in Bonwetsch, Hippolytus Werke I, 1897, pp. 232-235; read in the Greek)

stories.story: LEGEND (c. 400): the poet Prudentius says Hippolytus, once a follower of Novatus's schism, told the crowd at his death to return to the catholic church, and that the judge, hearing his name (which means loosed horses), had him torn apart by wild horses. It is borrowed from the Greek myth of Theseus's son Hippolytus and cannot be historical in this form.
stories.source: Prudentius, Peristephanon 11 (Latin, own reading); Catholic Encyclopedia (1910)

stories.story: In 1551 a seated marble statue was dug up on the Via Tiburtina with an Easter table and a list of his books carved on the chair; it was restored as "Saint Hippolytus". Twentieth-century study (Guarducci) showed the original figure was a woman, perhaps a personification; the head and upper body are Renaissance additions.
stories.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Wikimedia Commons file description; A. Handl, Louvain Studies 44 (2021)

temperament.trait: Self-appointed guardian of orthodoxy, conscious of apostolic authority
temperament.evidence: "But we, as being their successors, and as participators in this grace, high-priesthood, and office of teaching, as well as being reputed guardians of the Church, must not be found deficient in vigilance, or disposed to suppress correct doctrine."
temperament.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 1, Proemium

temperament.evidence: Of bishop Zephyrinus: "an ignorant and illiterate individual, and one unskilled in ecclesiastical definitions".
temperament.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 9 chapter 6

temperament.evidence: "And we, becoming aware of his sentiments, did not give place to him, but reproved and withstood him for the truth's sake."
temperament.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 9 chapter 6

temperament.evidence: He surveys every Greek school and sect before refuting them, and promises "we shall evince reserve in nothing"; he also computed Easter cycles and a world chronology (Eusebius, Church History 6.22).
temperament.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 1, Proemium

temperament.trait: Cautious about sacred things and about date-setting
temperament.evidence: On the end of the world: "we are obliged to discuss the matter of the times, of which a man should not speak hastily, because they are a light to him."
temperament.source: Fragments on Daniel, second fragment, section 4 (ANF)

genuine_lines.quote: This constitutes the import of the proverb, Know yourself; i.e., discover God within yourself, for He has formed you after His own image.
genuine_lines.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)

genuine_lines.quote: And you shall be a companion of the Deity, and a co-heir with Christ, no longer enslaved by lusts or passions, and never again wasted by disease. For you have become God
genuine_lines.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)

genuine_lines.quote: Do not devote your attention to the fallacies of artificial discourses, nor the vain promises of plagiarizing heretics, but to the venerable simplicity of unassuming truth.
genuine_lines.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)

genuine_lines.quote: There is, brethren, one God, the knowledge of whom we gain from the Holy Scriptures, and from no other source.
genuine_lines.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
genuine_lines.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)

genuine_lines.quote: the face of the fathers and the righteous is seen to be always smiling
genuine_lines.work: Against Plato, On the Cause of the Universe (Against the Greeks)
genuine_lines.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)

genuine_lines.quote: at this hour all creation rests for a certain moment, that all creatures may praise the Lord: stars and trees and waters stand still with one accord
genuine_lines.location: Easton chapter 36, on prayer at midnight
genuine_lines.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus (Cambridge University Press, 1934); public domain in the US (copyright not renewed, released by Project Gutenberg as eBook 61614) and in life-plus-70 countries (Easton died 1950)

misattributed.line: The Apostolic Tradition is Hippolytus's own church order of c. 215
misattributed.truth: The attribution is modern (early 20th century). Many specialists now treat it as an anonymous, layered compilation. Quote it as the church order traditionally linked to Hippolytus.

misattributed.line: On the End of the World, and On the Twelve Apostles and Seventy Disciples
misattributed.truth: Spurious; even the Ante-Nicene Fathers labels them pseudonymous.

misattributed.line: Hippolytus first fixed Christmas on 25 December (Commentary on Daniel 4.23)
misattributed.truth: The date appears in the manuscripts, but many scholars regard that line as a later insertion. Do not use it as a certain Hippolytus claim.

misattributed.line: Hippolytus was a Novatianist priest torn apart by wild horses
misattributed.truth: From Pope Damasus's epitaph and Prudentius (late 4th century). Novatian's schism began in 251, after Hippolytus's death, and the horses come from the Greek myth of Hippolytus.
The ancient chair carries his Easter tables and book list, but the seated figure was originally a woman; the head and bust are 16th-century restorations.
A later confusion with a martyr of Porto; Eusebius and Jerome did not know his see at all.

opinions.side_note: Against lax second chances (he did not deny repentance itself, but the ease and the source).
opinions.position: Against his bishop's easy pardon: Callistus let people believe that any sin was forgiven just by joining his congregation, and took in those Hippolytus had expelled.
opinions.quote: And he first invented the device of conniving with men in regard of their indulgence in sensual pleasures, saying that all had their sins forgiven by himself.
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Most people today side with Callistus's mercy; the rigorist minority sides with Hippolytus. A good pole against Cyprian and Callistus.

opinions.side_note: Pure-church side. The ark image is Callistus's argument, which Hippolytus quotes in order to attack.
opinions.position: He rejects Callistus's claim that the church, like Noah's ark, should hold clean and unclean alike; a church that offers communion to everyone indiscriminately has lost the right to call itself catholic.
opinions.quote: not discerning with whom they ought to communicate, but indiscriminately offering communion to all.
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Most churchgoers today prefer the "ark" or "field hospital" view; a strict-membership minority agrees with Hippolytus.

opinions.topic: new: leaders who sin should step down
opinions.position: A bishop who sins gravely must be deposed, and clergy who marry more than once should not keep their place; he condemns Callistus for relaxing both rules.
opinions.quote: About the time of this man, bishops, priests, and deacons, who had been twice married, and thrice married, began to be allowed to retain their place among the clergy.
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: "Leaders who fall should step down" is widely agreed today; the marriage rule is held only in some churches.

opinions.position: Using drugs to prevent or end pregnancy is murder, and a church that tolerates the unions that lead to it teaches "adultery and murder at the same time".
opinions.quote: Behold, into how great impiety that lawless one has proceeded, by inculcating adultery and murder at the same time!
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Splits the public sharply; the question is live and emotionally loaded, so use with care.

opinions.side_note: For open rebuke of leaders.
opinions.position: When a bishop teaches error, you must confront and resist him openly, even if everyone else goes along.
opinions.quote: And we, becoming aware of his sentiments, did not give place to him, but reproved and withstood him for the truth's sake.
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Splits people: some admire public challenge; others think disagreement with leaders should be private and loyal.

opinions.side_note: Suspicious of philosophy as a source, but thoroughly learned in it.
opinions.position: Heresies come from Greek philosophy, mystery cults and astrology rather than Scripture; yet he studied all of them in detail in order to expose them.
opinions.quote: but that their doctrines have derived their origin from the wisdom of the Greeks, from the conclusions of those who have formed systems of philosophy, and from would-be mysteries, and the vagaries of astrologers
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Splits people as Tertullian does, though Hippolytus models "study it to refute it" rather than "ignore it".

opinions.side_note: Contrast Tertullian, who refused to argue from Scripture with heretics (Prescription 19).
opinions.topic: new: the Bible is the only source for knowing God
opinions.position: All we know of God comes from the Holy Scriptures and nowhere else; we must believe as they teach, not as our own mind prefers.
opinions.quote: There is, brethren, one God, the knowledge of whom we gain from the Holy Scriptures, and from no other source.
opinions.work: Against the Heresy of One Noetus
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Splits Christians: many Protestants agree; Catholics and Orthodox add tradition; many others think God is known through nature, reason or experience too.

opinions.side_note: Strongly for free will and responsibility.
opinions.position: Human beings have real free will; that is why God gave a law, since you do not give laws to animals, only bridles and whips.
opinions.quote: For if man did not possess the power to will and not to will, why should a law be established? For a law will not be laid down for an animal devoid of reason, but a bridle and a whip
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Most people today agree; Reformed Christians and determinists push back.

opinions.side_note: An early statement of what the East calls theosis.
opinions.position: The goal of human life is to be made divine: obey God and you will become a companion of the Deity, deified and immortal.
opinions.quote: And you shall be a companion of the Deity, and a co-heir with Christ, no longer enslaved by lusts or passions, and never again wasted by disease. For you have become God
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Splits Christians: Orthodox and many Catholics embrace the language; many Protestants find it alarming.

opinions.topic: new: knowing yourself leads to God
opinions.position: To know yourself truly is to find God's image within you.
opinions.quote: This constitutes the import of the proverb, Know yourself; i.e., discover God within yourself, for He has formed you after His own image.
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Very appealing to modern people; some Christians worry it sounds like self-worship. A good splitter for a self-understanding site.

opinions.side_note: Against universal salvation. Attribution: this piece came down under Josephus's name, but Photius and modern scholars give it to Hippolytus.
opinions.position: Punishment for the wicked is endless; no prayer of friends can help them.
opinions.quote: No sleep will give them rest; no night will soothe them; no death will deliver them from punishment; no voice of interceding friends will profit them.
opinions.work: Against Plato, On the Cause of the Universe (Against the Greeks)
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Splits Christians roughly in half in many surveys; most non-believers reject eternal punishment.

opinions.side_note: Against date-setting and alarmism.
opinions.topic: new: predicting the end of the world
opinions.position: Do not speak hastily about the date of the end. By his reckoning it was still some 300 years off (500 years after Christ), and he tells of two church leaders whose predictions ruined their flocks.
opinions.quote: From the birth of Christ, then, we must reckon the 500 years that remain to make up the 6000, and thus the end shall be.
opinions.location: second fragment, section 6 (ANF); 4.24 in the full Commentary
opinions.translation: S. D. F. Salmond, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Nearly everyone now distrusts date-setting; the splitter is "the end is near and we should live as if it is" versus "not in our lifetime".

opinions.side_note: Sceptical of private revelations (a strong contrast with Perpetua and Tertullian).
opinions.position: Beware leaders who trust their own dreams and visions over Scripture; the Pontus bishop (own rendering of the Greek) trusted his own visions over Scripture and misled his whole church.
opinions.quote: he did not attend carefully to the Scriptures, but trusted rather the visions which he himself saw
opinions.translation: Own rendering from the Greek (Bonwetsch, Hippolytus Werke I, GCS 1897, p. 234): μὴ προσέχων δὲ ἀσφαλῶς ταῖς γραφαῖς, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ὁράμασιν οἷς αὐτὸς ἑώρα μᾶλλον ἐπίστευεν
opinions.original_text: μὴ προσέχων δὲ ἀσφαλῶς ταῖς γραφαῖς, ἀλλὰ τοῖς ὁράμασιν οἷς αὐτὸς ἑώρα μᾶλλον ἐπίστευεν (the scan OCR garbles γραφαῖς; the parallel Old Slavonic, translated into German on p. 235 of the same edition, reads: nicht lesend die Schrift, sondern den Traumgesichten schenkte er Glauben)
opinions.today: Splits Christians: charismatics trust present-day revelation more; many others share his caution.

opinions.topic: new: guarding sacred teaching from scoffers
opinions.position: Do not hand deep teaching over to unbelieving and mocking listeners; share it with those who want to live holy lives.
opinions.quote: Only see that you do not give these things over to unbelieving and blasphemous tongues, for that is no common danger. But impart them to pious and faithful men, who desire to live holily and righteously with fear.
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Splits people: open-access, share-everything culture disagrees; some believers feel holy things should not be exposed to ridicule.

opinions.side_note: Pacifist side. Authorship caution: the Apostolic Tradition was assigned to Hippolytus by modern scholars (Schwartz 1910, Connolly 1916); many now see it as a layered church order compiled over time, so treat it as the church order linked to Hippolytus, not his certain words.
opinions.position: A soldier who becomes a Christian must refuse to kill even under orders; a believer who seeks to join the army is to be rejected.
opinions.quote: If a catechumen or a believer seeks to become a soldier, they must be rejected, for they have despised God.
opinions.location: Easton chapter 16 (a soldier "must be taught not to kill men and to refuse to do so if he is commanded")
opinions.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus (Cambridge University Press, 1934); public domain in the US (copyright not renewed, released by Project Gutenberg as eBook 61614) and in life-plus-70 countries (Easton died 1950)
opinions.today: Most Christians today accept military service; historic peace churches agree with this rule.

opinions.side_note: Against Christians in office with the sword. Authorship caution: the Apostolic Tradition was assigned to Hippolytus by modern scholars (Schwartz 1910, Connolly 1916); many now see it as a layered church order compiled over time, so treat it as the church order linked to Hippolytus, not his certain words.
opinions.position: A magistrate or commander who wears the purple (with power of life and death) must resign before baptism.
opinions.quote: A military commander or civic magistrate that wears the purple must resign or be rejected.
opinions.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus (Cambridge University Press, 1934); public domain in the US (copyright not renewed, released by Project Gutenberg as eBook 61614) and in life-plus-70 countries (Easton died 1950)
opinions.today: Very few Christians today would bar believers from being judges or officials.

opinions.side_note: Against the entertainment trades of the day. Authorship caution: the Apostolic Tradition was assigned to Hippolytus by modern scholars (Schwartz 1910, Connolly 1916); many now see it as a layered church order compiled over time, so treat it as the church order linked to Hippolytus, not his certain words.
opinions.position: Actors, charioteers, gladiators and anyone who runs the games must give up the trade to be baptized.
opinions.quote: If a man is an actor or pantomimist, he must desist or be rejected.
opinions.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus (Cambridge University Press, 1934); public domain in the US (copyright not renewed, released by Project Gutenberg as eBook 61614) and in life-plus-70 countries (Easton died 1950)
opinions.today: One-sided against it today (acting is seen as a respectable job), though some Christians avoid certain entertainment industries.

opinions.side_note: Gentler than Tertullian on schoolmasters. Authorship caution: the Apostolic Tradition was assigned to Hippolytus by modern scholars (Schwartz 1910, Connolly 1916); many now see it as a layered church order compiled over time, so treat it as the church order linked to Hippolytus, not his certain words.
opinions.topic: new: jobs a believer should give up
opinions.position: Some jobs are incompatible with faith; others are tolerated if there is no alternative. A teacher of pagan literature to children should stop, but may continue if it is his only living.
opinions.quote: A teacher of young children had best desist, but if he has no other occupation, he may be permitted to continue.
opinions.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus (Cambridge University Press, 1934); public domain in the US (copyright not renewed, released by Project Gutenberg as eBook 61614) and in life-plus-70 countries (Easton died 1950)
opinions.today: The principle (some jobs are off-limits) splits people; the specific list is outdated.

opinions.side_note: A positive view of married sex, against purity scruples. Authorship caution: the Apostolic Tradition was assigned to Hippolytus by modern scholars (Schwartz 1910, Connolly 1916); many now see it as a layered church order compiled over time, so treat it as the church order linked to Hippolytus, not his certain words.
opinions.position: Marital intimacy does not defile; a married believer rising to pray at midnight need not purify himself again.
opinions.quote: He who has used the marriage bed is not defiled; for they who are bathed have no need to wash again, for they are clean.
opinions.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus (Cambridge University Press, 1934); public domain in the US (copyright not renewed, released by Project Gutenberg as eBook 61614) and in life-plus-70 countries (Easton died 1950)
opinions.today: Nearly everyone today agrees; not a splitter, but it softens the ascetic caricature.

opinions.side_note: Authorship caution: the Apostolic Tradition was assigned to Hippolytus by modern scholars (Schwartz 1910, Connolly 1916); many now see it as a layered church order compiled over time, so treat it as the church order linked to Hippolytus, not his certain words.
opinions.topic: new: praying in the middle of the night
opinions.position: Rise at midnight and again at cockcrow to pray, with your spouse if they believe; at that hour all creation pauses to praise God.
opinions.quote: At midnight arise, wash thy hands with water and pray.
opinions.translation: Burton Scott Easton, The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus (Cambridge University Press, 1934); public domain in the US (copyright not renewed, released by Project Gutenberg as eBook 61614) and in life-plus-70 countries (Easton died 1950)
opinions.today: Few do it; monks, some Orthodox and night-shift pray-ers do. Splits "sleep is holy rest" from "vigil is devotion".

opinions.side_note: Against enmity (a closing appeal, not a treatise on anger).
opinions.position: Stop hating one another and turn back quickly; Christ came to wash away sin and make humanity new.
opinions.quote: Be not therefore inflamed, O you men, with enmity one towards another, nor hesitate to retrace with all speed your steps.
opinions.translation: J. H. MacMahon, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5, ed. Roberts, Donaldson and Coxe (1886)
opinions.today: Universally agreed in principle; weak splitter.

sparring.over: Forgiveness of grave sins, discipline of clergy, marriages between women of rank and lower-class men, and the Trinity (Callistus called him a "Ditheist"; he called Callistus a Sabellian and "an impostor and knave")
sparring.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 9 chapters 6-7

sparring.over: Zephyrinus's public formula "I know that there is one God, Jesus Christ"; Hippolytus calls him ignorant, illiterate and "accessible to bribes"
sparring.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 9 chapter 6

sparring.with: Noetus of Smyrna and his follower Cleomenes
sparring.over: Modalism: that the Father Himself was born, suffered and died
sparring.source: Against the Heresy of One Noetus; Refutation Book 9 chapters 2-5

sparring.over: Modalism; Hippolytus says Sabellius listened to his admonitions until Callistus drew him back
sparring.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 9 chapter 6

sparring.with: Alcibiades of Apamea and the Elchasaites
sparring.over: A new book of revelation promising a second forgiveness of sins through a further baptism
sparring.source: Refutation of All Heresies, Book 9 chapters 8-12

sparring.over: Not a recorded quarrel: the two were exiled together to Sardinia in 235 and were evidently reconciled, since the Roman church buried and honoured both as martyrs
